sections.heading: When this job comes up
body: Customer has lawn grubs in their lawn. Mitch's service is called Lawn Grub Treatment. Past invoices read: "Lawn grub treatment using registered insecticide" with the lawn area in square metres, and "Larvae Treatment, cottage only".

In a lawn the damage usually comes from curl grubs (beetle grubs that eat the roots) or lawn armyworm (caterpillars that eat the leaves). Check which one it is before you treat. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW and Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch]
The job process, the never list, PPE and the free service period are in the Every job guide. [Mitch to confirm: does the free service period apply to this job?]

sections.heading: How to tell what is eating the lawn
rows: Large white or cream C-shaped grub with a brown head and six legs near the head. Lives in the soil and eats the roots. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW, not from Mitch]

Plants with eaten roots can wilt or go yellow. Dead grass pulls up easily. Birds digging at the lawn can be the first sign. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW and DPIRD Western Australia African black beetle guidance, not from Mitch]

A curl grub, about 25 mm when fully grown, with a brown or tan head. The adult is a glossy brown-black beetle about 14 mm. [Mitch to confirm: from Tasmanian DPIPWE African black beetle fact sheet, not from Mitch]
A real problem in newly sown lawns. The adults fly in late summer and autumn. [Mitch to confirm: from Tasmanian DPIPWE African black beetle fact sheet, not from Mitch]

Smooth, plump caterpillar up to about 40 mm, greyish brown with pale and dark markings. Hides at the base of the grass or under soil clods in the day, feeds at night. [Mitch to confirm: from Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch]
Leaves stripped and bare patches, with green-yellow pellet droppings. [Mitch to confirm: from Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch]
Dry or hungry grass can look the same. Rule these out before you blame grubs. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW, not from Mitch]
Looks like grub damage. Grubs are unlikely to do real damage unless there are lots of them. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW, not from Mitch]

items.text: Rule out dry or hungry grass first
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW, not from Mitch]

items.text: Tug the dead grass
items.detail: If it lifts out easily, the roots have probably been eaten. [Mitch to confirm: from DPIRD Western Australia African black beetle guidance, not from Mitch]

items.text: Dig a small patch at the edge of the damage and look in the top of the soil and the roots for white C-shaped grubs
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture) and Tasmanian DPIPWE African black beetle fact sheet, not from Mitch]

items.text: Look at the base of the grass and under soil clods for caterpillars, or look at dusk when they come out
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch]

items.text: Kids and pets off the lawn. Pet bowls and bedding moved
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch]

items.text: Cover fish ponds, barbecues and vegie gardens near the lawn. Close doors and windows
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch]

items.text: Rainwater tank: stop overspray getting onto the gutters and roof
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch]

items.text: Not on a rainy or windy day
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch] [Mitch to confirm: Mitch's own weather limits. No source gives the numbers]

items: Ask the customer to show you where the lawn is damaged
Take BEFORE photos of the damaged areas

items.text: Check it really is grubs (see How to check)
items.detail: Dry or hungry grass can look the same. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW, not from Mitch]

items.text: Work out the lawn area in square metres
items.detail: Past invoices give the area in m2. [Mitch to confirm: how you measure it]

items.text: Estimate the wind speed and direction before you start, and write it down. Note it again if the wind changes
items.detail: Outdoor spraying needs this in the record, and anything else the label says about weather. [Mitch to confirm: from the NSW Pesticides Regulation 2017 (record of use), not from Mitch. Check it is still the current version]

items.text: Treat the lawn
items.detail: [Mitch to confirm: how you apply it, and whether it is watered in] Do not water the garden after spraying, and check the label for how long to wait. [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch. Mitch to say whether his lawn jobs are watered in]

items.text: Apply per the product label. Never exceed label rates
items.detail: Never mix chemicals without checking the label first. If in doubt, call Mitch.

items: Keep chemicals away from food, children and pets
Note anything you could not treat or reach, and why

Customer given the re-entry time: follow the product label. The Every job guide says 1 to 2 hours once dry [Mitch to confirm: same as Every job (1 to 2 hours once dry) for this job?]
Service report left, or customer told it is being emailed

items.a: Often it's one of two things. Curl grubs are beetle grubs that live in the soil and eat the roots. Lawn armyworm are caterpillars that eat the leaves. We check which one you've got. [Mitch to confirm: from UNSW and Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch]

items.q: Why did the lawn go so fast?
items.a: Armyworm hide at the base of the grass in the day and feed at night, so you don't see them until the patches show. [Mitch to confirm: from Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch]

items.q: When can the kids and the dog go back on the lawn?
items.a: Keep them off while we treat. Follow the product label for when it's safe. We normally say 1 to 2 hours once it's dry. [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government) and the Every job guide, not from Mitch]

Follow the product label. Don't water straight after spraying unless the label says to. [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch. Mitch to say whether his lawn jobs are watered in]

It depends how much has been eaten. A good feed and water helps it recover, once the label says it's okay to water. [Mitch to confirm: from Business Queensland (written for crops and pasture), not from Mitch. It says generous nitrogen fertiliser and water help lawns recover. Check you are happy with this wording]

items.q: Why did you want to move the job for rain or wind?
items.a: Spraying outdoors on a rainy or windy day isn't recommended, so we pick a better day. [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government), not from Mitch]

sections.heading: Tell Mitch straight away if
sections.body: Call Mitch on 0432 181 689. After hours or urgent, call Mitch directly.

items.text: You apply the wrong chemical
items.detail: Stop immediately. Do not continue. Call Mitch.

items.text: There is a spill
items.detail: Follow the SDS procedure. Call Mitch immediately. Never leave a spill unattended.

items.text: Someone is hurt
items.detail: Treat the injury first. Call Mitch. Write down what happened.

items.text: The customer complains or gets aggressive
items.detail: Stay calm and do not argue. For a complaint, tell them Mitch will call them today. If they are aggressive, remove yourself. Call Mitch either way.

items.text: The customer asks for a quote on anything complex, or you are not sure
items.detail: Say "I'll need to get Mitch to come and have a look and provide a quote for that."

items.text: You see signs of termites or other pests outside this job
items.detail: Photograph it and tell Mitch. Termite quotes always go to Mitch.
